title: The end writes the memory.
dek: In a 1993 experiment, most people chose to repeat 90 seconds of cold water over 60, because the extra 30 ended a little warmer. When I look back at my week on Sunday, I am doing the same thing.
whyThisIdea: Toate ideile din backlog sunt marcate ca prea apropiate de articole publicate, așa că am adăugat una nouă, legată de faptul că azi e duminică, ziua în care îți faci bilanțul săptămânii: regula peak-end (Kahneman, experimentul cu apa rece din 1993 și studiul cu 682 de pacienți din 2003). Cifrele din experimente sunt verificabile, iar calculul cu notele pe zile e al tău, marcat clar ca presupunere.

entry.title: The end writes the memory.
entry.dek: In a 1993 experiment, most people chose to repeat 90 seconds of cold water over 60, because the extra 30 ended a little warmer. When I look back at my week on Sunday, I am doing the same thing.
body: “Nobody remembers the whole week. They remember the worst day and the last one.”

Have you ever asked yourself why a week can feel bad in your head when most of its days were actually fine? Today is Sunday, the 22nd of November, and Sunday is the day I look back at the week before I plan the next one. And almost every time, I do the same thing - I ask myself “how was it?” and the answer comes very fast, before I have even thought about Monday or Tuesday. So the question is: when I remember a week, what am I actually remembering? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at is called the peak-end rule. The idea is that when we judge an experience after it is over, we do not add up every moment of it. We mostly remember two things: the most intense moment, and how it ended. How long it lasted matters surprisingly little. I met it while reading about Daniel Kahneman, the psychologist who won the Nobel prize in economics in 2002, and it made me look again at every Sunday “how was it?” I ever answered.

Firstly, let’s split the title in two, the way I like to do. “The end” and “writes the memory”. The first half sounds obvious - of course the end is important, it is the last thing you saw. The second half is the strange part. It does not say the end is a part of the memory, it says the end writes it. The last few minutes of something get to decide what the whole thing was. And that means the version of the week that I carry into the next one is not the week I lived, it is a short summary written by its worst moment and its last one.

Secondly, let’s look at the experiment, because this is where it surprised me. In 1993, Kahneman and three colleagues, Barbara Fredrickson, Charles Schreiber and Donald Redelmeier, asked people to put one hand in cold water, twice. In the short trial, the hand stayed in water at 14°C for 60 seconds. In the long trial, it stayed at 14°C for the same 60 seconds and then for 30 seconds more, while the water was warmed up to 15°C. Still cold, still painful, just a little bit less. So the long trial is the short trial plus extra pain. Then they asked people which one they would rather repeat. A clear majority chose the long one. The title of their paper says everything: “When More Pain Is Preferred to Less”.

And it is not only a lab trick. Ten years later, Redelmeier, Kahneman and a colleague tested the same idea in a hospital, with 682 patients having a colonoscopy, which is a very unpleasant medical exam. For half of them, chosen at random, the doctor added a short extra interval at the end that was less uncomfortable. Those patients rated the final moments as less painful, 1.7 versus 2.5 out of 10, and they also rated the whole procedure as less unpleasant. Longer exam, better memory. The memory did not count the minutes, it counted the ending.

Now let’s bring it to my own week, because that is the part I can actually check. These numbers are my assumptions, not a measurement. Let’s say I give every day a mark out of 10. Monday 7, Tuesday 7, Wednesday 6, Thursday 7, Friday 2 (a test that went badly), Saturday 7, and Sunday 4, because I spent it worrying about Monday. If I calculate it properly:
Average of all 7 days: 40 ÷ 7 = 5.7
Worst day and last day: (2 + 4) ÷ 2 = 3

The week I lived was a 5.7. The week I remember, if the rule is right, is a 3. And now let’s change only one day. Same week, but on Sunday I do something I like, and it becomes a 7 instead of a 4:
Average of all 7 days: 43 ÷ 7 = 6.1
Worst day and last day: (2 + 7) ÷ 2 = 4.5

Look at what happened. Changing one day moved the real week by less than half a point, 3 ÷ 7 = 0.43. But it moved the remembered week by 1.5 points, about three and a half times more. I did not fix Friday, the test is still bad. I only fixed the ending, and the ending is the part that gets to write the summary.

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to. A rule this strong is a little bit dangerous, because it works just as well when someone else uses it on you. If the memory only keeps the peak and the end, then anybody who controls the end controls the memory - a holiday that finishes with a nice dinner, a course with an easy last week, an app that shows you something good just before you close it. And it can also be used to lie to yourself. A bad semester with a fun last weekend is still a bad semester. If I only care about the ending, I can make every week look good on Sunday and never notice that Wednesday has been a 3 for two months. <u>A good ending can be a gift or it can be a hiding place.</u>

So here is what I am going to do today, because it is Sunday and the week is already over. First, before I answer “how was it?”, I will write the seven marks down, one per day, so that the average gets a vote and not only the worst day. Second, I will protect the last part of the day, and of the week, a little bit more - not by making it perfect, just by not filling it with the things I dread. Ten minutes at the end that I actually like cost almost nothing and, if Kahneman is right, they change how I remember everything before them.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I really believe that most of my bad weeks were not as bad as I remember them, and that knowing about the peak-end rule is a cheap way to be a little bit fairer with myself. But I have to be honest about two things. My arithmetic with the marks is a simplification - the rule says the peak and the end matter most, not that memory is exactly their average, and I made up the marks. And there is something uncomfortable in managing my own memory, as if the goal is a nicer story and not a better week. Maybe the right use of the rule is not to make Sundays nicer, but to notice when only the Sundays are nice.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“Nobody remembers the whole week. They remember the worst day and the last one.”
